summary:
Putumayo department stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, while a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to custody are governed by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Enforcement lags far behind that framework. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia and flailing in a creek; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. No one had been arrested although police interrogated local residents, and President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently, with solidarity events held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025; the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025; more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, reported elsewhere as 41; and eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. Earlier fatal attacks recalled in the same reporting include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised and adjacent to Putumayo. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, a department sharing a border with Putumayo, flyer campaigns circulated on streets and by WhatsApp announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and name "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign run by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night. Discrimination limits trans women in the department mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The clearest illustrations of organised hostility come from outside Putumayo. The Millerey killing occurred in Bello, Antioquia, and drew a presidential order for an urgent investigation alongside solidarity events in several cities; the national toll of anti-trans killings is the context that bears on Putumayo rather than any Antioquia-specific finding.

Caquetá, which adjoins Putumayo, shows what the armed-group threat looks like on the ground: expulsion notices issued to individual trans women, flyer and WhatsApp campaigns naming LGBTI people as military targets, and a sex-trade and hairdressing economy into which trans women are concentrated. Guajira has produced a publicly posted kill list of named individuals since March 2024, demonstrating that the same tactics are in use in more than one region.

Colombia's formal protections and its homicide record run in parallel rather than in sequence. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 assessment described a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, and the Attorney General's figures for 2023, 2024 and 2025 all record lethal violence continuing under a regime that recognises self-declared gender markers and marriage equality.
localsOnly:
Residents change their sex marker by signing a document before a notary, a process available since June 2015 and applied without judicial examination, and the same route supports the "trans" and "non-binary" markers carried on national identification documents since November 2025.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree binds government institutions to procedural obligations on LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and in the treatment of victims of armed conflict, and the May 2018 executive decree extends guarantees into housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Residents in custody are covered by rulings on trans detainees, including the 2011 decision permitting a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup.

Economic marginalisation shapes daily life for trans residents: discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing or sex work, and residents in Caquetá have been forced to relocate after death threats from armed men. The comprehensive trans law still before the legislature in 2025 would alter resident protections if enacted.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no finding specific to Putumayo department. Every violence, threat and displacement claim recorded here comes from Antioquia, Guajira, Caquetá or national reporting, so the presence or absence of armed-group kill-list flyers inside Putumayo itself is unresolved and not sourced.

Whether any trans person has been killed in Putumayo in 2023, 2024 or 2025 is not sourced; national totals are given instead, and the breakdown by department is not available in this inventory. Whether the Attorney General's Office has opened any hate-crime investigation in the department is likewise unresolved.

Implementation of the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" markers at civil registries and notary offices in Putumayo is not sourced, and no reporting in the inventory confirms whether the comprehensive trans law under consideration in 2025 has since been enacted.
